name: Digital Multimeter
tagline: Measures volts, ohms, amps and continuity — the instrument every test begins with.
parts: Display — holds the reading so you can let go before you read it
Selector dial — volts, ohms, continuity, current; the setting decides the input impedance
COM jack — the reference terminal every measurement returns to
V/Ω/mA jack — for everything except high current
10 A jack — a separate, unfused shunt for heavy current
Test leads — fused on the current ranges, and rated for the voltage you are measuring
safety: The dial position matters more than the leads: measuring volts with the leads in the amps jack is a short circuit, and measuring resistance on a live circuit feeds the meter's own battery into the supply. Set the range before the probes touch anything, use 600 V CAT III or better leads on fixed wiring, and treat a reading of zero on a voltage range as a reason to prove the meter before you trust the circuit is dead. It is also not an insulation resistance tester: a multimeter pushes a few volts into a conductor, where an insulation resistance test applies 500 V and measures in megohms — which is why a meter can read a cable as fine when its insulation is already failing.

points.label: Display
points.detail: A digital readout is only as good as the range behind it: 188.8 on the 200 V range and 188.8 on the 1000 V range are different measurements, and a meter left on autorange can read a phantom tens of volts on an open circuit because its input impedance is so high it picks up capacitive coupling from a live conductor running alongside.

points.label: Selector dial
points.detail: The dial rewires the meter internally, which is why volts and ohms share a jack but the 10 A range does not. Turn it before you probe, not after: the classic mistake is measuring voltage with the leads still in the current jacks, which puts a near-short across the supply.

points.label: Input jacks (COM, V/Ω, 10 A)
points.detail: COM is the reference every measurement returns to; V/Ω/mA covers everything except heavy current, which has its own unfused 10 A shunt. The jacks are rated for a category as well as a current — CAT III 600 V for work on fixed wiring, never the CAT II lead set that came with a cheap meter.

points.label: Test leads and probes
points.detail: On a good lead set the probe tips are spring-loaded and the finger guards stop your hand sliding onto metal: that is what GS 38 asks for, and it is why a bare 4 mm probe on a plug-in lead has no business near a live board. Current ranges are fused in the meter; the leads themselves are not, so a lead rated for 600 V on a distribution board matters.

points.label: Housing and hold button
points.detail: A rugged case with a recessed display is not decoration — it is what survives being dropped off a step ladder. Hold or backlight lets you probe, let go, and then read the number, which is the whole point on a job where you cannot watch both the display and the probe tip at once.
